query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) to equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW induces microstructural modifications that improve room‐temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance while preserving high‐temperature mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that shows excellent strength at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C) but suffers from poor room-temperature ductility and has an irradiation resistance that is only computationally inferred.
generation.intervention: Subject NbMoTaW samples to a deep cryogenic treatment process after fabrication.
generation.conditions: Experimental evaluations conducted at room temperature and at high temperatures up to 1600 °C, with irradiation tests involving helium ion implantation at energy levels known to cause blistering and irradiation-enhanced precipitation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates, subgrain boundaries, or localized phase transitions induced by DCT that can increase the availability of active slip systems and serve as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
generation.mechanism: DCT is proposed to relieve residual stresses and induce subtle phase transformations or re-distribution of solute atoms, which adds additional slip systems that enhance ductility at room temperature. Concurrently, the new microstructural features are expected to trap and annihilate irradiation-induced defects, thereby reducing amorphization, blistering, and precipitation under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, DCT-treated samples should exhibit a significant increase in room-temperature ductility (e.g., higher elongation), maintain their high-temperature yield strength, and show reduced irradiation damage in terms of defect density, amorphization, and surface blistering.
generation.baseline: Untreated NbMoTaW displays excellent high-temperature mechanical performance but poor room-temperature ductility and unknown irradiation response, with prior evidence suggesting potential irradiation-induced amorphization and blistering in similar refractory HEAs.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be beneficial in the operational regime from room temperature up to 1600 °C and under irradiation conditions (helium ion implantation) that mimic the energy levels at which deleterious effects like blistering and enhanced precipitation have been previously observed.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether DCT will induce the predicted microstructural evolutions in NbMoTaW to the same extent as observed in other BCC HEAs (e.g., HfNbTaTiZr) and whether these changes will sufficiently mitigate irradiation-induced damage.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equal-atomic NbMoTaW samples: one set undergoes deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) and the other remains untreated. Conduct tensile testing at room temperature and at increments up to 1600 °C. Subject both sets to controlled helium ion irradiation at energies known to induce blistering and precipitation. Evaluate mechanical properties and inspect microstructures using nanoindentation, electron microscopy, and defect analysis.
measurements: Incidence and morphology of surface blistering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If DCT-treated NbMoTaW does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and a reduction in irradiation-induced defects and blistering compared to untreated samples, or if high-temperature performance is adversely affected, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy has wide application prospects as a biomedical material, and the use of laser additive manufacturing can solve the forming problems faced by the alloy. In view of the characteristics of the one-time forming of additive manufacturing methods, it is necessary to develop non-mechanical processing modification methods. In this paper, deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) is first applied to the modification of a HEA with BCC structure, then the post-processing method of DCT is combined with laser melting deposition (LMD) technology to successfully realize the coordinated improvement of forming and strength–ductility synergistic improvement in lightweight Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr alloy. The final tensile strength of the alloy after DCT treatment is 25% higher than that of the as-cast alloy and 11% higher than that of the as-deposited alloy, and the elongation is increased by 48% and 10%, respectively. In addition, DCT also achieves induced phase transition without additional deformation.Keywords: laser melting deposition, high entropy alloy, deep cryogenic treatment, 3D printing, defects, strength–ductility synergistic improvement
